reading.rtitle: The Real Price of an Executive MBA
paras: Ask a candidate what an executive MBA costs, and he will give you the fees. Although the fees are the number that everybody discusses, they are rarely the biggest cost. The biggest cost is time: for most programs, somewhere between fifteen and twenty hours a week, for almost two years. Economists call this the opportunity cost — the value of everything else those hours could have been used for. For a director who runs a company, that value is high.

Even though executive programs are designed for people who keep their jobs, the hours have to come from somewhere, and they usually come from evenings and weekends. Despite the flexible schedule, many graduates say that the first term was the hardest period, and that it took a toll on their families before it took a toll on their work. The company pays a price too: somebody has to make decisions during the residencies, when the director is on another continent.

The candidates who manage it best are not the ones with the most time. They are the ones who decide before they start: who at home is on board, what the family will cut back on, and who will run things at work while they are away. None of this makes the program easy. Even so, a sacrifice that was discussed in advance is very different from one that arrives by surprise in the middle of the first term.

listenings.text: Near the end of the interview I ask a question that surprises many candidates: who at home knows that you are applying, and what do they think? It is not a personal question for its own sake. Although the program is designed for people with full-time jobs, the hours come from somewhere, and they usually come from evenings and weekends that belonged to a family. Candidates who have not had that conversation tend to leave in the first term, despite being excellent professionals. So I want to hear that your family is on board, and I want to hear what you will cut back on. Even a simple answer is fine. What worries me is the candidate who tells me that nothing will change.

When I decided to apply, I was forty-seven, I ran a company with two hundred people, and I had two children in school. The fees were high, but the fees were not the hard part. Even though I had planned everything, the first term took a toll on everybody at home. I missed my daughter’s school play because of a finance exam, and I remember thinking that no degree was worth that. What saved the program for me was a conversation, not a plan. My wife and I sat down and agreed on three things I would never miss, whatever the calendar said. Despite the pressure, I kept all three for two years. If I did it again, I would have that conversation before I applied, not in the middle of the first term.
